title: Backup, recovery and imaging
summary: Learn the backup strategies a technician relies on, how to restore user data with File History and recover a system with wbadmin, and how imaging lets you rebuild a machine fast.
objectives: Explain the 3-2-1 backup rule and why it matters
Tell the difference between a file backup, a system image, and a recovery point
Restore user files with File History
Create and restore a system image backup with wbadmin
Describe how disk imaging speeds up rebuilding many machines
Decide which recovery method fits a given failure

quiz.q: What does the 3-2-1 backup rule recommend?
options: 3 copies of data, on 2 different media, with 1 copy off-site
quiz.why: 3-2-1 means keep three copies of your data, on two different types of media, with at least one copy stored off-site, so a single failure or disaster can't wipe everything.

quiz.q: A user deleted a single document yesterday and needs it back. Which is the quickest appropriate tool on Windows?
quiz.why: File History keeps versioned copies of user files, so a single deleted or changed document can be restored quickly without touching the rest of the system.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of a system image over a file-only backup?
options: It is smaller and faster to create
It restores the whole OS, apps and settings as one unit
quiz.why: A system image is a block-level snapshot of the whole drive, so restoring it brings back the operating system, installed applications and settings together — ideal after a disk failure.

quiz.q: Which command creates a system image backup on Windows?
quiz.why: wbadmin start backup creates a backup including a system image; the others repair files, check the disk, or wipe a disk respectively.

quiz.q: In one sentence, explain why imaging is useful when setting up many identical computers.
quiz.answer: You configure one machine perfectly, capture it as an image, and deploy that single image to many computers so they all start identical without repeating the setup each time.
quiz.why: Imaging captures a known-good build once and clones it to many devices, saving hours and guaranteeing consistency across a fleet.

quiz.q: Why should at least one backup copy be kept off-site or offline?
quiz.answer: So that a local disaster such as fire, theft, or ransomware that encrypts everything reachable on the network cannot destroy every copy of the data at once.
quiz.why: An off-site or offline copy is isolated from local failures and online threats, which is the whole point of the '1' in the 3-2-1 rule.

body_markdown:
## Backups exist for the bad day

Nobody appreciates a backup until a disk dies, a laptop is stolen, or ransomware locks every file. As a technician your job is to make sure that bad day is survivable. That means knowing the difference between backing up **files**, backing up a whole **system image**, and being able to **recover** when something fails. Get this right and a catastrophic failure becomes an inconvenience.

## The 3-2-1 rule

The industry shorthand is **3-2-1**: keep **3 copies** of your data, on **2 different media** (for example an internal disk and an external drive or cloud), with at least **1 copy off-site or offline**. The off-site copy is what saves you from fire, theft, or ransomware that encrypts everything it can reach on the network. A backup that sits next to the original on the same machine is barely a backup at all.

## File backups vs system images

There are two flavours you must keep straight. A **file backup** copies documents, photos and settings — small, frequent, easy to restore one item from. A **system image** is a block-level snapshot of the entire drive: operating system, installed apps and settings as one unit. You restore a file backup to get a document back; you restore an image to rebuild a whole machine after a disk failure.

On Windows, **File History** handles versioned file backups:

```powershell
# File History is configured in Settings, but you can drive the engine
FileHistory
# Check status from PowerShell
Get-WindowsFeature -Name FS-Data-Deduplication | Format-Table -AutoSize
```

To restore a single file, open **File History** from Control Panel, browse to the file, pick a version, and click the green restore button.

## System image with wbadmin

For a full image, `wbadmin` is the built-in command-line tool. Run it from an **elevated** prompt:

```cmd
:: Create a system image of C: onto drive E:
wbadmin start backup -backupTarget:E: -include:C: -allCritical -quiet

:: List the backups you have
wbadmin get versions
```

Sample output:

```cmd
Backup time: 16/06/2026 09:14
Backup target: Fixed Disk labelled E:
Version identifier: 06/16/2026-08:14
Can recover: Volume(s), File(s), Application(s), Bare Metal Recovery, System State
```

To recover a whole system, boot into the **Windows Recovery Environment** and choose **System Image Recovery**, pointing it at the image you created.

## Imaging for fleets

**Imaging** takes the system-image idea and scales it. You configure one machine perfectly — the **gold image** — capture it, then deploy that single image to many computers so they all start identical. Tools like DISM capture and apply Windows images (`.wim` files):

```powershell
DISM /Capture-Image /ImageFile:D:\gold.wim /CaptureDir:C:\ /Name:"Gold build"
```

This is how IT departments rebuild a broken laptop in twenty minutes instead of a day.

## Your task

On a test or virtual machine: turn on **File History** to an external or second drive, create a test document, then delete it and restore the previous version. Next, from an elevated prompt run `wbadmin get versions` to inspect any system backups present (or create one with `wbadmin start backup` if you have a spare target). Finally, write two or three sentences mapping each of these failures to the right recovery method: a single deleted file, a dead boot drive, and rebuilding ten identical machines.

slides.title: File History on Windows
bullets: Keeps versioned copies of user files.
Configured in Settings, points at a second drive.
Restore one file from Control Panel.
Pick a version, click the green restore button.
slides.narration: On Windows, File History handles versioned file backups. You point it at an external or second drive in Settings, and it quietly keeps versions of your files over time. To restore, open File History from Control Panel, browse to the file you want, choose the version by date, and click the green restore button. It's the fastest way to bring back one deleted or changed document.

slides.title: System image with wbadmin
bullets: wbadmin start backup creates the image.
Run it from an elevated prompt.
Target a separate drive, include C:.
wbadmin get versions lists your backups.
slides.code:
wbadmin start backup -backupTarget:E: -include:C: -allCritical -quiet
wbadmin get versions
slides.narration: For a full image, w-b-admin is the built-in command-line tool. Open an elevated prompt and run w-b-admin start backup, with backup-target colon E, include colon C, and all-critical. That captures a system image onto drive E. To see what backups you already have, run w-b-admin get versions. Each entry shows the backup time, the target, and what it can recover.

slides.title: Recovering a whole system
bullets: Boot the Windows Recovery Environment.
Choose System Image Recovery.
Point it at your saved image.
Brings back OS, apps and settings together.
slides.narration: To recover an entire system, you boot into the Windows Recovery Environment, often reached by interrupting startup a few times or from install media. From there choose System Image Recovery and point it at the image you created. It restores the operating system, applications, and settings together, so the machine comes back exactly as it was when you took the image.

slides.title: Imaging for fleets
bullets: Configure one perfect 'gold image'.
Capture it once with a tool like DISM.
Deploy the same image to many machines.
Rebuild a broken laptop in minutes.
slides.narration: Imaging scales the system-image idea up. You configure one machine perfectly, the gold image, then capture it and deploy that single image to many computers so they all start identical. The tool DISM captures and applies Windows images, the dot wim files. This is how an IT department rebuilds a broken laptop in twenty minutes instead of a day.

slides.title: Match the failure to the method
bullets: Deleted file -> File History.
Dead boot drive -> system image restore.
Many identical PCs -> deploy an image.
Always keep one copy off-site.
slides.narration: The skill is matching the failure to the right method. A single deleted file? File History. A dead boot drive? Restore the system image. Setting up ten identical machines? Deploy a gold image. And underneath all of it, the three, two, one rule: always keep one copy off-site or offline, because that's the copy that survives the worst day.

slides.narration: Let's recap. The three, two, one rule keeps three copies on two media with one off-site. File History restores single files. W-b-admin creates and restores system images. And imaging rebuilds many machines fast. Your task: on a test machine, turn on File History, create a document, delete it, and restore the previous version. Then run w-b-admin get versions to inspect any system backups, and write a few sentences mapping a deleted file, a dead boot drive, and ten identical machines to the right recovery method. See you in lesson eight.
